title: A living hope (1 Peter 1:3–9)
hookLine: born again into a living hope through the resurrection

cards: In Luke's Gospel, Peter warms himself at a fire in a courtyard and says, three times, that he doesn't know Jesus. Then a rooster crows, and he goes out and weeps.
Years later the same man, now a leader of the Church, writes to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey, people being mocked and pushed to the edges for their faith.
He could open with a warning, a plan, a word about his own failures. Instead, after a short greeting, the first thing out of his pen is a blessing, and the blessing is about hope.

teach.b: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy hath regenerated us unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead."
Lively: in older English, that meant living. The Greek says it plainly, a living hope. Not a wish.
Not optimism, which is a weather forecast about how things will probably turn out. Peter's hope is anchored in something that already happened: a tomb that was empty, a friend he saw alive again.
And he had his own reason to need it. On Easter morning, in Mark's Gospel, the message for the disciples names him in particular: go, tell his disciples and Peter.
Then Peter describes what the hope looks toward, an inheritance with three nots.
It can't perish. It can't be stained. It can't fade.

In Greek all three begin with the same little a-, meaning not. Peter doesn't pretend the present is easy. His readers are grieving in various trials for a while, and he compares their faith to gold tested by fire.
The hope doesn't remove the fire. It tells you what the fire is for.

teach.h: WHOM HAVING NOT SEEN, YOU LOVE.
teach.b: Then a line to the readers themselves: "Whom having not seen, you love."
Peter had seen. They hadn't. He's writing to people who love someone they've never laid eyes on, and he tells them their joy is real anyway.

how: Readings from the first letter of Peter are heard at Mass during the Easter season, and Catholics count hope as one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity, anchored in the resurrection of Christ.

o: the apostle who denied Jesus, then wrote of hope
the disciple who ran first to the empty tomb
the first bishop of Ephesus, a friend of Paul

games.q: Peter's living hope — tap the pairs.

s: a lively hope in the Douay-Rheims means a cheerful hope
in older English lively meant living. the Greek says a living hope.
Peter's letter is written to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey
he greets them in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia.
Peter says the living hope means trials won't come
he says they grieve in trials for a while; faith is gold tested by fire.

games.q: you're Peter, the one who denied Jesus three times. years later you write to Christians who are being mocked for their faith. how do you begin?
o: with an apology for your own failures.
with a blessing for the living hope of the resurrection.
with a warning about what's coming.
games.why: after a short greeting, Peter blesses God for a living hope, born of the resurrection. the man who denied Jesus writes first about hope.

practice: Notice what you're carrying right now, the trial, the worry, whatever's heavy, and let it be there without fixing it.
Underneath it, look for one hope bigger than this week, for someone you love, for the world, for yourself, and name it once, quietly.
If you pray, hold it beside Peter's living hope, the resurrection; if not, let the hope sit beside the weight, both of them real.

wordCard.voice: Peter. The apostle who denied Christ three times by a fire, and years later opened his letter with a blessing: a living hope born of the resurrection. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a living hope (1 Peter 1:3). the Douay-Rheims renders it a lively hope.

carryVoice: Your line: gold tested by fire. A hope that can't perish, stain or fade. See you tomorrow.
